Overall assessment: Viability is currently low and scalability is unproven. The concept is socially compelling and the three-part blend of hardware, curriculum and local space is creative, but the business model is a list of hoped-for revenue streams rather than a validated path to profit. Nearly every load-bearing assumption is untested.

Path to making money: Unclear. (1) Class fees: no prices set, and the target customers are low-income, so the company intends to keep fees low while carrying heavy fixed costs (rent, stoves, insurance, instructors). That yields thin or negative unit economics unless subsidized. (2) Restaurant recruiting fees: described as something they 'hope' for, with zero restaurant relationships, no letters of intent, and no evidence restaurants pay for entry-level hires they can already source freely; the industry's chronic hiring difficulty argues more for employer demand than for willingness to pay. (3) Grants: 'may apply' is not a plan; grant revenue is lumpy, competitive, tied to outcomes (placement/retention data they do not yet have), and makes the company dependent on nonprofit funding while organized as an S Corp, which is an awkward structure for grant eligibility. (4) Selling or leasing stoves: an entirely separate hardware business with different customers, margins and support needs, and a distraction at this stage. There is no budget, no cost of capital expenditure, no break-even calculation, and no projection, so the claim of break-even within two years is unsupported.

Key assumptions and their validity: (a) Smart stoves reduce instructor needs and 'pay for themselves': unsupported. Food safety, knife skills, sanitation, and supervision of open flame with teenagers and novices still require a qualified instructor, likely a certified chef, and liability and insurance costs may rise rather than fall. The team has no chef. (b) Demand: the market is sized as 'a small percentage of many people,' which is top-down reasoning with no data. Validation consists of friends and family saying the idea 'sounds interesting,' which is not evidence of willingness to pay or enroll. No pilot class, no waitlist, no students. (c) Certification as a barrier: food-handler cards are typically cheap, short, online courses; if that is the real credential requirement, a multi-class series may be more than the market needs, and the value proposition for the job-seeker may be weaker than assumed. Whether restaurants actually demand cooking experience beyond this for entry-level roles is untested. (d) Differentiation: the smart stove is the claimed moat, but it is a screen with timers and temperature prompts, which is easily replicated and is not a proprietary advantage. The 'local relationships' defense is asserted, not yet built. Nonprofit and community college programs are real incumbents with existing funding, employer ties and credibility. (e) Multilingual guidance is a genuine plus, but language support in cooking instruction is also achievable with bilingual instructors or printed/video aids at much lower cost.

Scalability: Weak as currently designed. Each site requires leased space, multiple stoves, equipment, insurance and staffing, making expansion capital intensive and slow, with returns dependent on low-fee, subsidized customers. Scale depends on replicable site economics and local employer/community partnerships, neither of which exists even once. The most scalable element, the stove guidance software or hardware licensed to other programs, is the least developed and would require a different go-to-market. Regulatory complexity (health department permitting, food safety, possibly workforce program accreditation) varies by jurisdiction and adds friction to replication.

Execution risks affecting viability: team is three students with no culinary, restaurant-operations or nonprofit/workforce expertise (Marisol's three years of part-time restaurant work is helpful but limited); no chef; only a single-stove prototype tested with friends; no website, customers, partners or budget; and the ask is for prize funding to commit to a lease and hardware before any demand validation, which is the wrong order of operations.

What would improve viability: run a low-cost pilot (one stove, a borrowed commercial or church kitchen, a 6-8 week class) to test demand, completion rates and instructor needs; secure 3-5 restaurant letters of intent specifying hiring volume and willingness to pay a fee; build a simple unit-economics model (cost per student, fee, subsidy gap, payback on stoves); partner with an existing nonprofit or workforce board rather than building standalone infrastructure; and decide whether the core business is a training service or a technology product, since trying to be both dilutes focus.

Conclusion: A promising social-impact idea with an attractive concept but no demonstrated demand, no economics, and heavy reliance on optimistic assumptions about subsidies and employer payments. It is pre-validation; viability and scalability cannot yet be credited, and the first priority should be cheap experiments, not capital spending on a lease and hardware.

Business plan text:

Cookpoint Academy
Cookpoint Academy
Executive Summary
Problem
Many immigrant families and teenagers in our city want to find work but do not know how to get
started. The restaurant industry is one of the biggest employers of immigrants and young
people, and it often has open positions. However, most restaurants require a food-handler
certification, and many want some cooking experience. The people who most need these jobs often
do not have access to affordable training. Community colleges can be far away, and their
classes may be expensive or held at inconvenient times. Language barriers also make it hard to
follow traditional cooking instruction. We believe there is a gap between the people who want
to work in food service and the training that is available to them in their own neighborhoods.
Solution
Cookpoint Academy is a neighborhood teaching kitchen that uses connected smart stoves to guide
students through cooking classes. Each stove has a screen that shows the student what to do
next, including the right temperature, how long to cook, and how to handle the food safely.
Because the stove guides the student, the class does not depend entirely on the instructor, and
students can learn at their own pace. The guidance can be shown in several languages, which
helps families who are still learning English. Students attend a series of classes that build
skills step by step. At the end of the series, they prepare for the food-handler certification
exam. After certification, we help connect students with restaurants that are hiring for entry
level positions.
We believe this combination of hardware, curriculum and a local physical space is a new way to
deliver job training. The teaching kitchen also becomes a place where the neighborhood can
gather, which we think will help us build trust with families.
Market
The market for Cookpoint Academy is immigrant families and teenagers who are interested in
working in restaurants. There are many immigrants in our metropolitan area, and a large share
of them work in food service or want to. There are also many teenagers looking for their first
job. If even a small percentage of these people enrolled in our classes, the market would be
large. The restaurant industry is also growing and often reports difficulty finding workers,
which suggests there is demand for trained employees. We have not yet conducted a formal market
study, but we have talked informally with friends and family members who said the idea sounds
interesting. We plan to do more research once we have funding.
Business Model
Cookpoint Academy will earn revenue in several ways. First, students or their families will pay
a class fee for each series of classes. Second, we hope to receive payments from restaurants
that hire our graduates, similar to a recruiting fee. Third, we may apply for grants from
workforce development programs and foundations. Fourth, we may eventually sell or lease our
smart stove system to other training programs and schools. We have not yet decided on exact
prices. Because our target students may have limited income, we expect to keep class fees low,
and we believe that grants and restaurant payments can make up the difference. The smart stoves
are a significant cost, but we believe they will pay for themselves over time because they
allow us to run more classes with fewer instructors.
Competition
Our competitors include community college culinary programs, nonprofit job training
organizations, and online cooking videos and courses. Community colleges offer more advanced
training but are often expensive and far from the neighborhoods we serve. Nonprofits offer

valuable programs, but many have long waiting lists and limited space. Online courses are cheap
but do not give students hands-on practice or help with finding jobs. We believe Cookpoint
Academy is different because we combine hands-on cooking with smart technology and job
placement in one local place. We do not believe any other organization in our area offers
exactly this combination. We recognize that larger organizations could copy our approach, but
we think our local relationships will give us an advantage.
Team
Marisol Echeverria-Tran is our chief executive. She is a business major at our university and
has worked part time in restaurants for three years. She leads strategy, partnerships and
fundraising.
Dwayne Okonkwo-Hale is our chief technology officer. He is a computer engineering student who
designed and built our prototype smart stove guidance system. He leads hardware and software
development.
Priyanka Venkataraghavan is our head of programs. She is studying education and nutrition and
is responsible for designing the class curriculum and preparing students for certification.
We do not yet have a professional chef on the team, but we plan to hire or partner with one. We
also plan to recruit advisors from the restaurant industry and from workforce development
organizations.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined our core business concept and formed a legal entity as an S Corp. Dwayne
has built a first prototype of the smart stove guidance system, which displays steps and timers
on a screen connected to a single stove. We have tested the prototype with a small group of
friends, who said it was easy to use. We have not yet run a real class, signed up any students,
or partnered with any restaurants. We do not yet have a website.
Our financial plan is still early. We estimate that opening our first teaching kitchen will
require a space to rent, several smart stoves, kitchen equipment, insurance, and money to pay
instructors. We believe the total startup cost will be significant, though we have not yet
prepared a detailed budget. We do not currently have revenue. We have personally contributed a
small amount of money to form the company and build the prototype. Over the next two years, we
hope to open one kitchen, enroll a few hundred students, and reach break-even, although we have
not yet built a projection to show how this will happen.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for prize funding from this competition to help us rent a space and buy the first
set of smart stoves and kitchen equipment. We would also welcome mentorship from judges and
advisors with experience in restaurants, education, and hardware. In particular, we would like
help with building a detailed budget, understanding food safety regulations, and finding
restaurants willing to hire our graduates. We would also appreciate introductions to local
community organizations and grant programs. We believe that with the support of this
competition, Cookpoint Academy can begin to help immigrant families and teenagers build careers
in food service, while building a company that grows over time.

Question: Comment on the viability and scalability of the business model and strategy. Address whether the company has a clear path to making money and growing, and evaluate the validity of the entrepreneur's assumptions.
